text:
Maya: Quick follow-up to the CP separation RFC. Proposal: move away from permanent VPC peering for control plane access and adopt a stitchless credential-exchange model for private endpoints. Agents would obtain short-lived signed tokens and use them to establish mTLS with CP front-tier. Pros: fewer peering attachments to manage, simpler route tables, lower baseline cost for many tenants. Cons: more frequent auth operations and potential transient reconnect latency when agents rotate creds.

Simon: I like reducing long-lived peering. Two immediate asks: (1) token lifecycle/rotation details, (2) how will reconnects affect tail latency for bursty workloads?

Maya: Rotation plan: tokens minted by a token-service with TTL ~5 minutes. Agents refresh proactively before expiry or on reconnect. Token issuance happens against a CP front-tier cache (L1) to avoid touching slow stores on every request. Expected reconnect overhead: an extra 1-2 RTTs during the exchange, so typical reconnect ~100-250ms; steady-state traffic shouldn't be affected because inference KV caches remain local to the agent.

Alex: Perf/scale note: token-service must be lightweight. Recommend: L1 token cache + per-tenant rate bucket, signer-proxy collocated with L1 to avoid per-request remote KMS calls, and a batched KMS signing path. Also consider a lease extension mechanism so agents can renew without a full mint handshake if within a small window.

Patrick: Operational risks: if token-service misbehaves, we could cause wide agent disconnects. Must have: canary rollout, a clear fallback path (automatic peering/dedicated-connector for affected tenants), and robust telemetry (mint latency, error rate, reconnects, and token rejection reasons). Also document an emergency toggle to revert tenants to peering quickly.

Maya: Implementation sketch: (a) token-service stateless API that reads tenant policy from a cached config store, (b) signer-proxy running in CP front-tier that holds an HSM/KMS-backed signing key and signs tokens locally, (c) agents support fallback: if token mint fails N times or token validation fails, agent tries an existing peering path if configured.

Simon: Identity mapping question: peering implies network-level isolation. With stitchless tokens we must encode both identity and permitted network/material scope. Proposal: token payload includes tenant_id, allowed-scopes (control.read, control.exec), and allowed-egress-cidrs. CP enforces scopes on every request and uses the egress list to validate any sideband operations.

Maya: Example token (simplified): ```{
  "sub": "tenant:acme-corp",
  "iat": 1742133000,
  "exp": 1742136000,
  "scopes": ["control:read","control:exec"],
  "egress": ["10.2.0.0/16","10.2.128.0/17"]
}``` Signed by signer-proxy with KMS key. The CP front-tier validates claims and enforces policy.
